For the First Time (Kim Weston album)

interviews.label: Slide Hampton
interviews.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

interviews.label: Slide Hampton
interviews.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: She played really good, and she wrote music that weighs as much as this building. That’s some of the heaviest music I ever heard. It was heavy. The men’s arrangements would sound little peep, peep, peep, around her.
quotes.summary: Hampton said Liston was the main arranger and real musical director of Gillespie's band, that she played very well and wrote 'music that weighs as much as this building', next to which the men's arrangements sounded like 'peep, peep, peep'.

quotes.quote: And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head was just — they had my head spinning.
quotes.summary: Hampton recalled that when he joined Gillespie's band Liston was the musical director, and the band's arrangements were so good he did not dare write for it himself.

quotes.quote: Melba Liston was the musical director. I had to go there. I had to go there and get kicked, kicked and beat-up on. I did it. They taught me a lot in there.
quotes.summary: Hampton recalled that Liston was musical director of Gillespie's big band when he joined, a band 'way over my head' where he was 'kicked and beat-up on' and taught a lot.

quotes.quote: I didn’t know that she was as heavy musically as she was. I got in that band. I learned it real fast. Musically, she was heavy.
quotes.summary: Hampton said he first worked with Liston in Dizzy Gillespie's band and quickly learned how musically heavy she was.

quotes.quote: I remember when I played with the Dizzy Gillespie group and I was playing arrangements by Quincy Jones, by Dizzy himself, Ernie Wilkins, Melba Liston, Benny Golson.
quotes.summary: Hampton listed Liston among the great arrangers (with Quincy Jones, Gillespie, Ernie Wilkins and Benny Golson) whose charts he played in Gillespie's band and learned harmonic resolution from.

quotes.quote: It was Melba, and Chuck Connors, who played with Duke’s band, and another trombone player.
quotes.summary: Hampton named Liston in the trombone section of Gillespie's band with Chuck Connors and a 'Willie', calling them all very good players.

quotes.quote: Melba, being the arranger that she was, she definitely was going to write something for a trombone choir.
quotes.summary: In a long account of trombone choirs, Hampton remarked that Liston, 'being the arranger that she was', was certain to write for one.

she_said.summary: Bryant recalled that Slide Hampton was in the trombone section on one of Liston's own record dates, which Liston acknowledged as 'a different Company altogether'; after her stroke Liston said she had tried turning her trombone around to blow it like Slide Hampton, without success.
she_said.one_liner: had him in her trombone section on record
she_said.her_quote: I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t
she_said.bryant_quote: But you had two separate ’bone sections on two different record dates. One was around Christmas time – they both were around Christmas time – one around the 22nd, one around the 24th. One you had Slide Hampton, Frank Rehak.

people.name: Randy Weston
albums: Live at the Five Spot (Randy Weston album)

interviews.label: Randy Weston
interviews.title: Randy Weston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this. She was in a wheelchair, she had been paralyzed on one side, and she can no longer play the trombone. I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know? But, it turned out her aunt Thelma was a computer specialist and Melba started studying the computer and how to write the music with her left hand.
quotes.summary: Weston said only Liston could arrange 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', recounting how, though paralyzed on one side and in a wheelchair after her stroke, she was goaded by him into the work and learned to write music by computer with her left hand.

quotes.quote: So this is not the first time this has happened with Melba. Unfortunately, she has had problems with illness. But, her spiritual strength is so powerful.
quotes.summary: Weston recalled that Liston's arrangements for his 1959 Five Spot date with Coleman Hawkins and his 1985 Montreal concert arrived from her hospital bed in California just in time, and praised the power of her spiritual strength despite her illnesses.

quotes.quote: Melba Liston did all the arrangements, by the way.
quotes.summary: Weston noted in passing that Liston did all the arrangements for the African night of his Montreal Jazz Festival residency.

quotes.quote: Melba did the arrangements for that.
quotes.summary: Weston mentioned that Liston did the arrangements for his 'Khepera' recording.

she_said.summary: Liston said she met Randy Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie at Birdland, arranged his music (including Little Niles) for some forty years with complete freedom, and credited him with pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
she_said.one_liner: arranged his music for 40 years
she_said.her_quote: I’ve been writing for Randy. I’m still writing for Randy. I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

interviews.label: Curtis Fuller
interviews.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship. I've seen her sit on the bandstand and cry.
quotes.summary: Fuller called his relationship with Liston in Quincy Jones's band a beautiful one and recalled seeing her sit on the bandstand and cry.

quotes.quote: But, I love every moment that I had with Melba, Patty Bowen and I have some young kids.
quotes.summary: After a long digression about Judy Garland, Fuller said he loved every moment he had with Liston and Patti Bown.

quotes.quote: Oh, I loved every moment of it
quotes.summary: Fuller said he loved every moment of working with Liston and that when he first met her he did not know Gerald Wilson was her husband.

people.name: Benny Powell
people.image: Count Basie and His Orchestra performs in Helsinki 1962 (JOKAHBL3E C04-11).tif

quotes.quote: Melba Liston is responsible for the arrangements.
quotes.summary: Powell said Liston was responsible for the arrangements in Randy Weston's band, which he described as sparse frameworks built around the solos.

quotes.quote: Oh, she had a birthday two days ago, Melba Liston. Wonderful woman.
quotes.summary: Powell noted Liston's recent birthday and called her a wonderful woman, adding that she now lived in New York, was wheelchair-bound, and was very close to Randy Weston.

quotes.quote: She’s been here for about two or three years. She’s been wheelchair bound for a little while, but she and Randy are very close
quotes.summary: Powell said Liston had moved to New York two or three years earlier, had been wheelchair-bound for a while, and was very close to Randy Weston.

she_said.summary: Bryant said Powell was one of the trombonists on Liston's first 'Melba and her 'Bones' record date; Liston answered that she had girls first and did not confirm him.
she_said.bryant_quote: On your first one you had Bennie Green, Al Grey, Benny Powell.

people.name: Quentin Jackson
albums: Further Adventures of Jimmy and Wes
Roll 'Em: Shirley Scott Plays the Big Bands

interviews.label: Butter Jackson
interviews.title: 61539_Butter Jackson oral history interview

quotes.quote: So I went to Atlantic City and played with Melba Liston. She had a band up there, for Kim Weston.
quotes.summary: Jackson recalled playing in Atlantic City in a band Liston led for singer Kim Weston, and in the next breath called her 'a great trombonist, too'.

quotes.quote: And Kim Weston, she -- so Melba had the band for Kim Weston.
quotes.summary: Jackson repeated that Liston had the band for Kim Weston that he went up to play in.

quotes.quote: Well, the trumpets -- the trombones, rather, was Melba Liston, Jimmy Cleveland, and we picked up AAKE PERSSON Okie Pearson, a Swedish trombone player.
quotes.summary: Jackson named Liston first in the trombone section of Quincy Jones's European touring band, with Jimmy Cleveland and Åke Persson.

interviews.label: Mary Lou Williams
interviews.title: 53571_Mary Lou Williams oral history interview

quotes.quote: Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great."
quotes.summary: Williams recounted that Gillespie sent Liston to check on her playing, that Liston reported back that 'Lou played some chords' worth hearing, and that when Gillespie praised arrangements for Newport Liston said they were Williams's own and she had only taken them down.

quotes.quote: Dizzy called and Melba and all the musicians were trying to get me out.
quotes.summary: Williams said Gillespie, Liston and other musicians were all trying to coax her back to performing.

people.name: Al Grey
albums: The Al Grey – Billy Mitchell Sextet

interviews.label: Al Grey
interviews.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

quotes.quote: But we had such a tremendous band that every one of those guys who came out of there are stars today, the ones that are left and all like that, and that was like Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly, and Phil Woods and Melba Liston and Billy Mitchell, who I brought into Count Basie’s band see because Lockjaw left.
quotes.summary: Grey named Liston among the members of Dizzy Gillespie's 'tremendous' big band, all of whom he said became stars.

she_said.summary: Liston said Al Grey played trombone in her group Melba Liston and Company and had 'been everywhere I've been'.
she_said.one_liner: had him on trombone in her group
she_said.her_quote: Then I had trombone – Al Grey. He played trombone with me. He’d been everywhere I’ve been. He comes in there once in a while.

people.name: Abbey Lincoln
albums: Love Having You Around: Live at the Keystone Korner Vol. 2

interviews.label: Abbey Lincoln
interviews.title: Abbey Lincoln — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music. Rare.
quotes.summary: Lincoln, dismissing the idea of a women's history in jazz, singled Liston out as the rare woman who comes to the music for the music.

she_said.summary: Asked about Abbey Lincoln, Liston said she was fine and that she still wrote for her now and then.
she_said.one_liner: singer she still wrote for
she_said.her_quote: Oh, she’s fine. I write for her now and then.

interviews.label: Teddy Edwards
interviews.title: 61520_Teddy Edwards oral history interview

quotes.quote: Melba Liston was with the band. She was writing and playing her trombone with the band.
quotes.summary: Edwards recalled hearing Gerald Wilson's band at Shepp's Playhouse, where Liston was writing for the band and playing trombone, and where he first met 'all of that gang'.

quotes.summary: Akiyoshi recalled that Liston was playing trombone in Gillespie's big band when she sat in with it in Boston.

people.name: Ernie Wilkins
people.description: American jazz saxophonist, bandleader and music arranger
albums: Bursting Out with the All-Star Big Band!

she_said.summary: Liston named Wilkins as one of the arrangers she was "real close" to, recalled him among the men in Gillespie's band on the State Department tour, and said she no longer heard his current writing.
she_said.one_liner: fellow arranger and close friend
she_said.her_quote: Arrangers, we all friends. Ernie Wilkins and all of us real close. I write the soul music, more or less, and they write the swing and bop stuff.

she_said.summary: Liston named Persip as probably the drummer on the Randy Weston album she arranged and played on, and agreed when Bryant asked whether he wanted her to write for his big band.
she_said.one_liner: probably drummed on her Randy Weston album
she_said.her_quote: And he and probably Charli Persip – can’t think of the bass player now. It’s a nice album.

she_said.summary: Liston called Kelly a fine pianist and said she had been supposed to marry him, but he died in Canada.
she_said.one_liner: was supposed to marry him
she_said.her_quote: Yeah. Wynton’s a fine pianist. Oh dear. I think we were – I was supposed to marry him, but he died over there in Canada or somewhere.

she_said.one_liner: was in Gillespie's touring band with him
she_said.her_quote: I don’t hear Benny Golson’s and Randy – I mean Ernie’s – I don’t hear those things, so I don’t know whether they’re doing that or not.

she_said.her_quote: Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy

she_said.her_quote: Yeah, and I loved his.
she_said.bryant_quote: How was it when you wrote with Oliver Nelson? He’s a hell of an arranger too.

she_said.summary: Bryant noted that Billy Mitchell's saxophone entry was set up by Liston's arrangement on a Gillespie-band recording; Liston's "Yeah" answered a question about writing for drums, not about him.
she_said.bryant_quote: like when Billy Mitchell came in on that saxophone, you had set it up. He came in, and Dizzy.

people.name: Britt Woodman
albums: Bursting Out with the All-Star Big Band!
Ray Brown with the All-Star Big Band

she_said.summary: Bryant said Liston began adding men such as Britt Woodman to her women's group; Liston's reply named the group and other players but not Woodman.
she_said.bryant_quote: But then you did start another group for girls, and then you started adding guys, like Britt Woodman.

she_said.summary: Liston told how she arrived in New York to find Dizzy had kept her chair empty for a week, how he silenced the doubters in his 1956 band by having them play one of her arrangements, that 'he was so good', and that she only later realized how much he did to keep the band together.
she_said.one_liner: trombonist and arranger in his big band
she_said.her_quote: He said, “Go on and take one of those arrangements out and see if they can play it.” Two or three bars later, he said, “Now who’s the …”

she_said.summary: Liston named Copeland among the players on the Randy Weston album she arranged and played on.
she_said.one_liner: recorded with him on Randy Weston's album
she_said.her_quote: It’s the best thing. I’m on it. Johnny Griffin, and Ray Copeland.

she_said.summary: Bryant said Rehak and Slide Hampton were in one of the trombone sections on Liston's Christmas-time record dates; Liston recalled it as "a different Company altogether".
she_said.one_liner: played on one of her trombone record dates
she_said.her_quote: Oh. That was a different Company altogether. I forgot about that.
she_said.bryant_quote: But you had two separate ’bone sections on two different record dates. One was around Christmas time – they both were around Christmas time – one around the 22nd, one around the 24th. One you had Slide Hampton, Frank Rehak.

people.name: Ernie Henry
people.image: Fats Navarro, Charlie Rouse, Ernie Henry, Tadd Dameron (Gottlieb 06541).jpg

she_said.summary: Bryant said Liston made a record with alto saxophonist Ernie Henry; Liston answered "Yeah" and went on to talk about Wynton Kelly.
she_said.one_liner: made a record with him
she_said.bryant_quote: Ernie Henry. You did a record with Ernie Henry, right? Good alto player.

she_said.summary: Liston said West played bass on the Gillespie records and later conducted the Montreal strings on the Randy Weston album she arranged, "quite well".
she_said.one_liner: conducted her strings arrangements in Montreal
she_said.her_quote: Yeah, but on that he was conducting. He was conducting quite well.

she_said.summary: Bryant said Green was one of the trombonists on Liston's first 'Melba and her 'Bones' record date; Liston answered that she had girls first and did not confirm him.
she_said.bryant_quote: On your first one you had Bennie Green, Al Grey, Benny Powell.

she_said.summary: Liston said she wrote for Dinah Washington, who gave her no problems, and contrasted her "soul, soul, soul" and choice of soul songs with Gloria Lynne's ballads.
she_said.one_liner: wrote arrangements for her
she_said.her_quote: Dinah – soul, soul, soul, but Gloria’s soul too, but it’s a different way. They come after me differently. I don’t know how to say it. When I write for Dinah – uh. And when I write for Gloria – it’s oo.

she_said.summary: Liston named Griffin as playing on the Randy Weston album she wrote, and listed "Johnny Griffin" among the things she had written before CDs.
she_said.one_liner: recorded with him on Randy Weston's album
she_said.her_quote: I’ve got a bunch of things. Johnny Griffin and all the things I wrote before CDs

people.name: Charles Mingus
people.description: American jazz double bassist, composer and bandleader (1922–1979)

interviews.label: Charles Mingus
interviews.title: 67802_Charles Mingus oral history interview

she_said.summary: Liston said she wrote one or two things for Mingus long ago, knew him out in Los Angeles, that he was "all music" with her, and that she left holes in her writing for him.
she_said.one_liner: wrote one or two things for him
she_said.her_quote: Mingus was all music with me, but I haven’t written for him in such a long, long time I can’t even remember how he was or anything. He was all right

interviews.label: Elvin Jones
interviews.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

she_said.summary: Liston said Elvin Jones came down to Jamaica with his group while she was teaching there and played for her students.
she_said.one_liner: brought his group to play for her students
she_said.her_quote: He had a band then and he had a band now, and he’s married to a Japanese – Elvin Jones. Elvin came down with his group.

she_said.summary: Bryant said John Coltrane was in Dizzy Gillespie's band when Liston first joined it, and Liston agreed.
she_said.one_liner: was in dizzy's band with him
she_said.bryant_quote: Is that the band with John Coltrane in it?

she_said.summary: Liston brought up bassist Major Holley herself when talking about the friends who stood by her, recalling that after her stroke he took her downtown and helped her pick out and buy her first computer.
she_said.one_liner: helped her buy her first computer
she_said.her_quote: He went with me and picked out my first computer.

she_said.summary: Specs Wright appears only in the transcriber's summary of Bryant naming members of the Dizzy Gillespie band Liston joined; Liston's reply (also summarised) does not mention him.
she_said.one_liner: named as a bandmate in Dizzy's band

people.name: Thelonious Monk
people.image: Thelonious Monk, Minton's Playhouse, New York, N.Y., ca. Sept. 1947 (William P. Gottlieb 06191).jpg

she_said.summary: Liston said she wrote for Monk, called it a great honor, and explained that because he did things on the piano nobody else did she had to leave spaces in her writing for him.
she_said.one_liner: wrote arrangements for him, leaving spaces
she_said.her_quote: Monk is a piano player and he does things with the piano that nobody else does, and I have to leave spaces and stuff for him.

she_said.summary: Bryant played Austin Cromer singing Liston's arrangement of If You Could See Me Now with Gillespie's band; Liston confirmed she wrote it.
she_said.one_liner: arranged If You Could See Me Now
she_said.bryant_quote: Austin Cromer sings your arrangement of If You Could See Me Now.

people.name: Billy Eckstine
people.image: Portrait of Billy Eckstine, New York, N.Y., between 1946 and 1948 (LOC).jpg
albums: At Basin Street East (Billy Eckstine and Quincy Jones album)

she_said.summary: Liston recalled that when she finally found the club to join Dizzy Gillespie's band, Billy Eckstine was standing out front and told her Dizzy had kept her chair empty for a whole week.
she_said.one_liner: found him out front when she joined Dizzy
she_said.her_quote: Right on the corner. Billy Eckstine was out front. He said, “…, where you been? We’ve been looking for you. Dizzy’s had the chair empty for a whole week.”

she_said.summary: Liston said she loved Ellington's arrangements but denied imitating anyone, and that she could excerpt Duke and Basie for the State Department tour because she had played with them or listened to them all the time.
she_said.one_liner: loved his arrangements, but wrote from her soul
she_said.her_quote: I loved them, but I don’t have anybody – I do it all from my soul, and if it sounds like somebody, well it sounds like somebody.

she_said.summary: Bryant guessed that the high line on the 1973 Little Niles track might be a trumpeter such as Jon Faddis; Liston replied that it was a mouthpiece and said nothing about Faddis.

people.name: Leonard Feather
people.description: British-American jazz musician and jazz writer (1914–1994)
people.image: Kitty Kallen and Leonard Feather swap Armenian vittles, 1945.jpg

she_said.summary: Liston said Feather got her a record date, that she had to record one of his tunes, and that she was not satisfied with some of the results, which were never released.
she_said.one_liner: got her a record date
she_said.her_quote: He was the one that got me the record date, but the record company was

she_said.summary: Liston said she worked for Ray Charles for two or three years, rejected his reputation for giving women a hard time — he was "just always nice" — and noted a woman now played trombone in his band.
she_said.one_liner: worked for him two or three years
she_said.her_quote: They were saying, Ray Charles, turn off the lights and give this woman a fit and all that. I said, no. We were together – I worked for him for two or three years

she_said.summary: Bryant mentioned Shorter only to identify an airplane crash (the one that killed his wife); Liston established no connection with him.
